2. Power the aircraft completely off, remove the battery from the aircraft, and place the aircraft body in a protective case; remove or fold propellers if the design allows and use a gimbal/camera cover to prevent damage.

3. Pack all spare lithium batteries in your carry-on only (not in checked bags). Protect each battery’s contacts (original caps, terminal covers, or nonconductive tape) and place each in a separate pouch/LiPo-safe bag to prevent short-circuits.

4. Keep battery capacities within typical carry-on limits (commonly ≤100 Wh per battery without airline approval; higher-capacity spares often require airline approval and quantity limits). If you’re unsure, check the Wh rating printed on the battery.

5. Pack the remote controller and charging gear so they’re easy to remove for screening if you have a connection; keep tools (multi-tools, blades, large wrenches) out of carry-on if they’re not permitted.

6. After landing at Washington Dulles (IAD), stay seated until your row is called, then deplane with the aircraft case and carry-on kept closed; do not power anything on in the jet bridge or terminal.

4. Pack batteries correctly: put each battery in an individual protective sleeve or LiPo-safe bag, tape/cover exposed terminals, and ensure batteries cannot be crushed or shorted by other items.  
5. If you’re arriving from outside the U.S., have travel documents ready for entry at Washington Dulles (IAD): passport/visa or ESTA (as applicable), and any required proof of onward travel.

9. Go through U.S. Customs. If you bought the drone or major accessories abroad, declare them if required. Do not attempt to conceal high-value items; fines and delays are common for non-declaration.  
10. If you have a connecting flight, follow signs for “Connecting Flights/TSA Security” and be ready to remove the drone case from your bag if TSA requests a closer look. Keep batteries in your carry-on during any re-screening.
